vignette:
Cassandra Mireille, a 37-year-old musician of mixed French-Canadian and Indigenous heritage, presented for her initial intake following a terrorist attack she survived at an outdoor music festival eighteen months ago. She had been performing on a secondary stage when a series of explosions tore through the main grounds. In the chaos that followed, she lay pressed against the metal scaffolding of her stage, unable to move, tasting the acrid chemical smoke that rolled across the field and hearing the screams of people she could not see. The smell of burning, the metallic tang on her tongue, the vibration of the ground - these were the textures of the worst forty minutes of her life, and they were textures she could not leave behind.

In the months following the attack, Cassandra's memories of the event remained extraordinarily vivid and multi-sensory in quality. She described them not as recollections but as re-entries - moments in which the full sensory architecture of the festival grounds reconstituted itself around her without warning. She could taste the smoke again, feel the cold scaffolding under her palms, hear the particular pitch of the crowd's panic. These were not dim impressions but experiences of startling clarity and totality, arriving with the force of the present tense. When the memory returned, it did not feel like remembering; it felt completely real across every sense at once.

Cassandra works as a session musician and performs at small venues around her city. The occupational consequences of her symptoms became apparent within weeks of returning to work. Rehearsal spaces, with their enclosed acoustics and the smell of stage equipment, had become unpredictable territory. During a session six months after the attack, a sudden loud feedback shriek from an amplifier triggered a full flashback - she was back at the festival, certain the attack was resuming. She left the session without explanation and did not return to that studio for two months. Her difficulty concentrating, which she had initially hoped was temporary, had begun to affect her ability to sight-read and hold complex arrangements in working memory - skills that had previously been effortless. Colleagues noticed. She became irritable in ways that surprised even her, snapping at a bandmate during a rehearsal over something minor, and later sitting in her car unable to account for the intensity of her own anger.

It was within this context of persistent re-experiencing that Cassandra's beliefs about herself and the world had quietly but thoroughly reorganized. Each time the memory returned with its full sensory force - unbidden, uncontrollable - she took it as evidence that she was fundamentally changed, that her mind was no longer trustworthy, and that the world she had inhabited before the attack had been a kind of naïve fiction. She had come to believe that people were not what they seemed - that the ordinary crowd at a festival, the strangers at a venue, even acquaintances, concealed something unknowable and potentially dangerous. These appraisals, in turn, seemed to keep the trauma close. When she found herself scanning a room for exits or watching the faces of strangers with suspicion, the act of vigilance itself seemed to drag the memory forward - as if her threat-monitoring mind could not separate the present environment from the festival grounds, collapsing the distance between then and now and pulling the flashback closer.

She had begun to feel that she no longer belonged anywhere - not on stage, not in the social world of musicians she had inhabited for fifteen years, not even fully in her relationship, where her partner's patience she experienced as something she did not deserve and could not sustain. She was certain she had no future in any recognizable form. These convictions deepened the sense of being permanently marked, which in turn made the memories feel more total, more defining - as though the vividness of what she remembered confirmed the hopelessness of what lay ahead.

What finally brought Cassandra to seek help was a conversation with her partner, who told her quietly one evening that he was frightened - not of her, but for her. She arrived at the intake appointment hoping, with some difficulty, that something could be recovered. What she feared most was that nothing could.
